py-func: A function is a named block of code you can run again and again just by writing its name. Real programs are built from small functions: one computes a price, one checks an email address, one formats a line of a report. ### Defining and calling a function You create a function with the keyword def (short for define), then a name, then round brackets, then a colon. The indented lines below form the function's body. Defining a function does not run it. The body runs only when you call the function, by writing its name followed by brackets. ~~~python def say_hello(): print("Hello!") print("Nice to meet you.") print("Before the call") say_hello() say_hello() ~~~ - Line 1: def creates a function called say_hello. The empty brackets mean it needs no information. Nothing is printed yet. - Lines 2 to 3: the body, indented by 4 spaces. Python stores these lines for later. - Line 4: back at the left edge, so this line is outside the function. It runs now and prints Before the call. - Line 5: calls the function. Python jumps into the body, prints its two lines, then comes back here. - Line 6: calls it again, so the two lines are printed a second time. ### Parameters, arguments and return Most functions need some input and produce a result. The names inside the brackets of the def line are parameters: empty slots. The values you write in the brackets when you call the function are arguments: they fill the slots, in order. The keyword return ends the function and sends a value back to the place where it was called. ~~~python def area(width, height): result = width * height return result small = area(3, 4) print(small) print(area(10, 2) + 1) ~~~ - Line 1: defines area with two parameters, width and height. - Line 2: multiplies them and stores the product in result, a variable that only exists inside the function. - Line 3: return hands result back to the caller, and the function stops. - Line 4: calls area(3, 4). The arguments fill the slots: width is 3 and height is 4. The call returns 12, which is stored in small. - Line 5: prints 12. - Line 6: a call can be used anywhere a value can. area(10, 2) becomes 20, then 20 + 1 is printed: 21. ### Printing is not returning print() only shows a value on the screen: the caller gets nothing back. A function that ends without return gives back the special value None, which means "no value". ~~~python def show_double(n): print(n * 2) def give_double(n): return n * 2 a = show_double(5) b = give_double(5) print(a, b) ~~~ - Lines 1 to 2: show_double prints twice its parameter but returns nothing. - Lines 3 to 4: give_double returns twice its parameter and prints nothing. - Line 5: the call prints 10 on the screen, but there is no return, so a gets None. - Line 6: nothing is printed; b gets the returned value 10. - Line 7: prints None 10. Only a returned value can be reused by other code, and the lesson checks test your functions by what they return. ### Default values and keyword arguments A parameter can have a default value, written name=value in the def line. If the caller leaves that argument out, the default is used. When calling, you can also name the arguments, like punctuation="!". These are keyword arguments, and their order no longer matters. ~~~python def welcome(name, punctuation="."): return f"Welcome, {name}{punctuation}" print(welcome("Ada")) print(welcome("Bo", "!")) print(welcome(punctuation="?", name="Cy")) ~~~ - Line 1: name is required; punctuation is optional and defaults to ".". - Line 2: builds the text with an f-string and returns it. - Line 3: only one argument, so punctuation uses its default. Prints Welcome, Ada. - Line 4: the second argument replaces the default. Prints Welcome, Bo! - Line 5: keyword arguments, in any order. Prints Welcome, Cy? Parameters with a default must come after the ones without. ### Returning early from an if chain A function can contain several return lines. The first one reached ends the function. So an if / elif chain can return a different answer for each range, and a last return catches everything left over. Functions can also use the result of other functions. ~~~python def speed_label(kmh): if kmh < 30: return "slow" elif kmh < 90: return "normal" return "fast" def to_kmh(meters, seconds): return round(meters / seconds * 3.6, 1) s = to_kmh(500, 20) print(s, speed_label(s)) print(speed_label(29.9), speed_label(30)) ~~~ - Lines 1 to 6: speed_label checks the ranges from the lowest up. Below 30, it returns "slow" and stops right there. Otherwise, below 90 returns "normal". If neither matched, line 6 runs and returns "fast". No else is needed: a return already ended the function. - Lines 7 to 8: to_kmh divides meters by seconds, multiplies by 3.6 to get km/h, and rounds to 1 decimal with round(). - Line 9: 500 / 20 is 25.0, times 3.6 is 90.0, so s is 90.0. - Line 10: prints 90.0 fast, because 90 is not below 90. - Line 11: 29.9 is slow, but exactly 30 is normal. Watch where the boundary values land. Reminder: ** raises to a power, so x ** 2 is x squared, and it is computed before / and *. ### Common mistakes - Using print instead of return: the value shows on screen, but your function returns None. - Forgetting the colon after def name(...), or forgetting to indent the body. - Defining a function and never calling it: nothing happens. - Testing ranges in a jumbled order. Start from the smallest threshold with <, so each branch only sees what is left. ### Recap - def name(parameters): defines a function; name(arguments) calls it. - return value sends a result back and stops the function. No return means None. - param=default makes an argument optional; name=value in a call is a keyword argument. - The first return reached wins, which keeps if / elif chains short.
py-args: Sometimes you cannot know in advance how many values a function will receive: a total of any number of prices, a log line with any extra details. Python has special parameters for that, plus a short way to write tiny functions for sorting. ### *args: any number of positional arguments A parameter written with one star, like *args, collects all the positional arguments (the ones without a name) into a tuple. The name after the star is up to you; args is just the usual choice. ~~~python def show(*items): print(items) print(len(items), "item(s)") show("a", "b", "c") show(42) show() ~~~ - Line 1: *items means "put every argument into a tuple called items". - Line 2: prints the tuple. - Line 3: len() works on tuples just like on lists. - Line 4: three arguments, so items is ('a', 'b', 'c') and the count is 3. - Line 5: one argument gives a one-item tuple, shown as (42,). The comma marks it as a tuple. - Line 6: no arguments gives an empty tuple () and a count of 0. ### Using the collected values A tuple works with everything you used on lists: for loops, len(), max(), min(), and sum(), which adds up all the numbers in a collection and gives 0 for an empty one. ~~~python def average(*scores): if len(scores) == 0: return 0 return sum(scores) / len(scores) print(average(12, 15, 18)) print(average()) print(sum((1, 2, 3)), sum(())) ~~~ - Line 1: every argument goes into the tuple scores. - Lines 2 to 3: with no scores, return 0 early, because dividing by 0 would crash. - Line 4: sum(scores) adds them up, then we divide by how many there are. - Line 5: 12 + 15 + 18 is 45, divided by 3: prints 15.0. - Line 6: no arguments, so the early return gives 0. - Line 7: sum() on a tuple directly gives 6, and on an empty tuple gives 0. ### **kwargs: any number of keyword arguments Two stars, like **kwargs, collect every keyword argument (name=value) into a dictionary. The names become the keys, as strings, and the values become the values. ~~~python def profile(**info): print(info) for key, value in info.items(): print(key, "is", value) profile(name="Ada", city="London", age=36) ~~~ - Line 1: **info means "put every keyword argument into a dict called info". - Line 2: prints {'name': 'Ada', 'city': 'London', 'age': 36}. - Lines 3 to 4: .items() gives the key and value pairs, printed one per line. - Line 5: the call. The keys keep the order you wrote them in. ### Sorting keys and joining text sorted() on a dictionary gives a list of its keys in alphabetical order. "sep".join(list_of_strings) glues strings together with sep between them. With a list comprehension, they turn a dict into a tidy line of text. ~~~python def tags(**options): keys = sorted(options) print(keys) parts = [f"{k}:{options[k]}" for k in keys] print(parts) return " | ".join(parts) print(tags(size="L", color="red", qty=2)) ~~~ - Line 1: collects the keyword arguments into the dict options. - Line 2: sorted(options) gives the keys in order: ['color', 'qty', 'size']. - Line 3: prints that list. - Line 4: the comprehension builds one string per key, looking up each value with options[k]. The f-string turns the number 2 into text. - Line 5: prints ['color:red', 'qty:2', 'size:L']. - Line 6: " | ".join(parts) returns color:red | qty:2 | size:L. - Line 7: prints the returned text. Inside join() you may drop the square brackets: " | ".join(f"{k}:{options[k]}" for k in keys) gives the same result. Without brackets it is a generator expression: it hands the strings to join one by one instead of building a list first. ### lambda: a tiny function in one line lambda creates a small function without a name: lambda parameters: expression. It returns the value of the expression automatically, with no return keyword. It is handy when you need a function only once. ~~~python square = lambda n: n * n def square_def(n): return n * n print(square(4), square_def(4)) ~~~ - Line 1: builds a function that takes n and gives back n * n, and stores it in square. - Lines 2 to 3: the very same function written with def. - Line 4: both calls give 16: prints 16 16. ### key=: telling sorted, max and min what to compare sorted(), max() and min() accept a key= argument: a function applied to each item to get the value to compare. The items themselves come back unchanged. A lambda is the usual way to write that function. ~~~python products = [("pen", 1.5), ("bag", 25.0), ("mug", 8.0)] by_price = sorted(products, key=lambda p: p[1]) print(by_price) print(sorted(["kiwi", "fig", "banana"], key=len)) print(max(products, key=lambda p: p[1])) print(min(products, key=lambda p: p[1])[0]) ~~~ - Line 1: a list of tuples, each holding a name and a price. - Line 2: for each tuple p, the key is p[1], its price. The list is sorted from the lowest price to the highest. - Line 3: prints [('pen', 1.5), ('mug', 8.0), ('bag', 25.0)]. - Line 4: key=len passes the built-in len function itself (no brackets), so words are ordered by length: ['fig', 'kiwi', 'banana']. - Line 5: the tuple with the highest price: ('bag', 25.0). - Line 6: the cheapest tuple, then [0] takes its name: pen. Add reverse=True to sorted() to get the largest first. ### Common mistakes - Writing key=len() with brackets: that calls len right away. Pass the function itself. - Forgetting that *args is a tuple and **kwargs is a dict. - Calling sorted() on tuples without key=: tuples are compared by their first item, here the name. - Forgetting the star in the def line: def total(nums) accepts exactly one argument. ### Recap - *args collects extra positional arguments into a tuple; **kwargs collects keyword arguments into a dict. - sum(), len(), sorted() and join() work directly on what you collected. - lambda x: expression is a one-line function. - key= tells sorted, max and min what to compare.
py-rec: Recursion is when a function calls itself. It is the natural way to handle data that contains smaller copies of itself: folders inside folders, comments with replies, lists inside lists. ### A function that calls itself Every recursive function needs two parts. A base case: a situation simple enough to answer directly, which stops the calls. And a recursive case: the function calls itself on a smaller problem, getting one step closer to the base case each time. ~~~python def countdown(n): if n == 0: print("Go!") return print(n) countdown(n - 1) countdown(3) ~~~ - Line 1: defines countdown with one parameter. - Lines 2 to 4: the base case. When n is 0, print Go! and stop. A bare return just ends the function. - Line 5: otherwise, print the current number. - Line 6: the recursive case: call countdown again with a number one smaller. - Line 7: countdown(3) prints 3 and calls countdown(2), which prints 2 and calls countdown(1), which prints 1 and calls countdown(0), which prints Go!. Each call has its own private n. Use Step through to watch four separate calls, each with its own value. ### Returning values from recursive calls Recursion gets powerful when each call returns a value that the call before it uses. Here we add up 1 + 2 + ... + n. The sum up to n is n plus the sum up to n - 1, and the sum up to 0 is 0. ~~~python def sum_to(n): if n == 0: return 0 return n + sum_to(n - 1) print(sum_to(3)) print(sum_to(10)) ~~~ - Lines 2 to 3: the base case: the sum up to 0 is 0. - Line 4: the recursive case: n plus the answer to the smaller problem. Python must finish sum_to(n - 1) before it can do the addition. - Line 5: sum_to(3) waits for sum_to(2), which waits for sum_to(1), which waits for sum_to(0). That one returns 0. Then the waiting calls finish in reverse order: 1 + 0 = 1, then 2 + 1 = 3, then 3 + 3 = 6. Prints 6. - Line 6: prints 55. The same shape with multiplication instead of addition gives the factorial: the factorial of 5 is 5 x 4 x 3 x 2 x 1. Think about what the base case must return for a product: a number that changes nothing when you multiply by it. ### What happens without a base case If the function never reaches a base case, it keeps calling itself until Python gives up: ~~~text RecursionError: maximum recursion depth exceeded ~~~ Make sure every call moves toward the base case, for example with n - 1, never n itself. ### isinstance: what kind of value is this? To walk through nested lists, you must know whether an item is a list (go deeper) or a plain value. isinstance(value, type) returns True if the value is of that type, otherwise False. ~~~python print(isinstance([1, 2], list)) print(isinstance(7, list)) print(isinstance("hi", str)) print(isinstance(7, int)) ~~~ - Line 1: [1, 2] is a list: True. - Line 2: 7 is a number, not a list: False. - Line 3: str is the type of text: True. - Line 4: int is the type of whole numbers: True. ### append versus extend Two list methods add things to a list. append(x) adds x as one single item, even if x is itself a list. extend(other_list) adds each item of other_list separately. ~~~python a = [1, 2] a.append([3, 4]) print(a) b = [1, 2] b.extend([3, 4]) print(b) ~~~ - Line 2: the whole list [3, 4] becomes one item. - Line 3: prints [1, 2, [3, 4]]. - Line 5: the items 3 and 4 are added one by one. - Line 6: prints [1, 2, 3, 4]. ### Recursion on nested lists Now combine the pieces. This function counts every plain value in a list, however deeply nested. For each item: if it is a list, ask the same function to count inside it; otherwise count 1. ~~~python def count_values(items): total = 0 for item in items: if isinstance(item, list): total += count_values(item) else: total += 1 return total print(count_values([1, 2, 3])) print(count_values([1, [2, [3, 4]], 5])) print(count_values([[], [[]]])) ~~~ - Line 2: each call starts its own counter at 0. - Line 3: looks at the items one by one. - Lines 4 to 5: a sub-list is handled by a recursive call, and the count it returns is added to total. - Lines 6 to 7: anything else counts as one value. - Line 8: returns this call's total to whoever called it. - Line 9: no nesting: prints 3. - Line 10: the outer call counts 1, then calls itself on [2, [3, 4]]. That call counts 2 and calls itself on [3, 4], which returns 2, so the middle call returns 3. Back at the top: 1 + 3 + 1 = 5. - Line 11: empty lists contain no values: prints 0. The base case is hidden here: a list with no sub-lists makes no further calls. To build a flat list instead of a count, start from an empty list instead of 0, and pick the right list method in each branch. ### Common mistakes - No base case, or a call that does not get smaller: RecursionError. - Forgetting to return the result of the recursive call, so the answer is lost on the way back. - Using append where you meant extend, which puts a whole list inside your list. - A wrong base value: 0 is right for a sum, but would turn every product into 0. ### Recap - A recursive function calls itself on a smaller problem. - The base case answers directly and stops the chain of calls. - Each call has its own variables; results come back in reverse order. - isinstance(x, list) tells you when to go deeper into nested data.
py-errors: Real programs meet bad data all the time: someone types "abc" where a number was expected, a value is zero, a key is missing. Exceptions let your code notice these problems and decide what to do, instead of crashing. ### What an exception looks like When Python cannot do something, it raises an exception: it stops the program and prints an error report called a traceback. The last line names the exception type and explains the problem. ~~~text Traceback (most recent call last): File "main.py", line 1, in n = int("abc") ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'abc' ~~~ Common types: ValueError (right type but bad value, like int("abc")), ZeroDivisionError (dividing by zero), KeyError (a missing dict key), TypeError (the wrong type, like "a" + 1). ### try and except Put risky code in a try: block. If an exception happens there, Python skips the rest of the block and jumps to the matching except block instead of crashing. If nothing goes wrong, the except block is skipped. ~~~python for text in ["12", "abc", "7"]: try: n = int(text) print("Got the number", n) except ValueError: print("Not a number:", text) print("Program still running") ~~~ - Line 1: tries three strings in turn. - Line 2: starts the protected block. - Line 3: int("12") works and n becomes 12. For "abc", int() raises a ValueError right here. - Line 4: runs only if line 3 succeeded, so it is skipped for "abc". - Lines 5 to 6: run only when a ValueError happened in the try block. Prints Not a number: abc. - Line 7: the loop finished normally. Without try, the program would have stopped at "abc". ### The error message and several except blocks except SomeError as e: stores the exception in the variable e; printing e shows its message. You can stack several except blocks for different types, and Python uses the first one that matches. ~~~python prices = {"pen": 1.5, "bag": 25.0} for item, people in [("bag", 5), ("pen", 0), ("hat", 2)]: try: share = prices[item] / people print(item, "costs", share, "each") except ZeroDivisionError as e: print("Cannot split", item, "between 0 people:", e) except KeyError as e: print("Unknown item:", e) ~~~ - Line 1: a small dict of prices. - Line 2: three test cases; each tuple is unpacked into item and people. - Line 4: looks up the price, then divides. For ("bag", 5), share is 5.0. - Line 5: prints bag costs 5.0 each. - Lines 6 to 7: for ("pen", 0), dividing by 0 raises ZeroDivisionError, and e holds the message division by zero. - Lines 8 to 9: for ("hat", 2), prices["hat"] raises KeyError; printing e shows the missing key, 'hat'. ### else and finally Two optional blocks complete the picture. else: runs only if the try block raised nothing. finally: runs every time, error or not, which is perfect for clean-up. ~~~python for text in ["3", "x"]: try: n = int(text) except ValueError: print(text, "is invalid") else: print(text, "doubled is", n * 2) finally: print("checked", text) ~~~ - Line 3: works for "3", raises for "x". - Lines 4 to 5: run for "x" only. - Lines 6 to 7: run for "3" only, printing 3 doubled is 6. - Lines 8 to 9: run in both rounds. The order is always: try, except, else, finally. ### try inside a function A return inside try or except works like anywhere else. This lets a function hand back a fallback value when something goes wrong. ~~~python def to_number(text): try: return float(text) except ValueError: return None print(to_number("2.5")) print(to_number("two")) print(to_number("two") is None) ~~~ - Line 3: if float() succeeds, its result is returned at once. - Lines 4 to 5: if it raises ValueError, the function returns None instead. - Line 6: prints 2.5. - Line 7: prints None. - Line 8: is None is the proper way to test for None: prints True. ### raise: signalling your own errors Sometimes a value is fine for Python but wrong for your program, like a quantity of 0. raise ValueError("message") creates an exception and throws it, which stops the function immediately. And when a function does not catch an exception, it travels up to whoever called the function, who can catch it there. ~~~python def parse_quantity(text): qty = int(text) if qty < 1: raise ValueError("quantity must be at least 1") return qty for text in ["4", "0", "lots"]: try: print("OK:", parse_quantity(text)) except ValueError as e: print("Rejected", text, "because:", e) ~~~ - Line 2: for "lots", int() already raises ValueError. The function has no try, so the exception travels out to the caller by itself. - Lines 3 to 4: for "0", the conversion works but the value is too small, so we raise our own ValueError. The function stops; line 5 does not run. - Line 5: only reached for good values. - Lines 6 to 10: the caller catches both kinds of failure the same way. Prints OK: 4, then two Rejected lines with their messages. Good to know: int("") (empty text) also raises ValueError, but int("-3") works and gives -3, so rejecting negative numbers is your job. ### Common mistakes - A bare except: with no type: it also hides typos and bugs in your own code. Name the exception you expect. - Catching an error and doing nothing, so problems vanish silently. - Putting too much code inside try. Keep only the lines that can fail. - Forgetting that raise stops the function: code after it in the same block never runs. ### Recap - An exception stops the program unless something catches it. - try / except Type as e catches it; else runs on success, finally always. - raise ValueError("why") rejects bad input yourself. - Uncaught exceptions travel up to the caller.
py-files: Programs often need data that lives longer than the program itself: a to-do list, a log, a report. Text files are the simplest way to read data in and save results out. ### Opening and reading a whole file open(name) opens a file and gives you a file object, a handle you read from. The with statement opens it, gives it the name written after as, and closes it automatically when the indented block ends, even if an error happens. f.read() returns the whole content as one string. ~~~python with open("notes.txt") as f: text = f.read() print(text) print(len(text), "characters") ~~~ - Line 1: opens notes.txt for reading and names the file object f. - Line 2: reads everything into the string text. - Line 3: we are outside the with block, so the file is closed, but text keeps its value. Prints the four notes. - Line 4: counts the characters, including the invisible line breaks. Each line of a text file ends with a newline character, written "\n" in Python. It is what makes the text jump to the next line. ### Reading line by line A file object can go in a for loop: each round gives the next line as a string, still ending with "\n". strip() removes it, together with any spaces at both ends. ~~~python with open("notes.txt") as f: for line in f: print(len(line), line.strip()) ~~~ - Line 1: opens the file. - Line 2: line is "buy coffee beans\n" in the first round, then the next line, and so on. - Line 3: len(line) includes the newline (17 for the first line), while line.strip() is the clean text. Why strip? print() adds its own line break, so printing the raw line would leave an empty line after each one. ### Writing and appending open(name, "w") opens a file for writing. The second argument is the mode: "r" to read (the default), "w" to write (it creates the file, or empties it if it already exists), "a" to append (add to the end). f.write(text) writes a string. It does not add a line break, so you add "\n" yourself. ~~~python with open("shopping.txt", "w") as f: f.write("milk\n") f.write("eggs\n") with open("shopping.txt", "a") as f: f.write("bread\n") with open("shopping.txt") as f: print(f.read()) ~~~ - Line 1: creates shopping.txt and opens it for writing. - Lines 2 to 3: write two lines, each with its own \n. - Line 4: opens the file again, in append mode: the existing content stays. - Line 5: adds a third line at the end. - Lines 6 to 7: read it back and print milk, eggs, bread. With "w" on line 4 instead, milk and eggs would be gone. ### enumerate: numbering items as you loop enumerate(collection) gives you pairs of (position, item) in a for loop. Positions start at 0, or at any number you choose with start=. ~~~python colors = ["red", "green", "blue"] for i, color in enumerate(colors): print(i, color) for i, color in enumerate(colors, start=1): print(f"Color #{i} is {color}") ~~~ - Line 2: each round unpacks a pair into i and color: (0, "red"), then (1, "green"), then (2, "blue"). - Line 3: prints 0 red, 1 green, 2 blue. - Line 4: start=1 makes the counting begin at 1. - Line 5: prints Color #1 is red, Color #2 is green, Color #3 is blue. ### Putting it together: filter, then save A common job: read lines, keep only the useful ones, write the result to a new file. A list comprehension with an if filters lines. A blank line strips down to the empty string "", and an empty string counts as false in an if, so if line.strip() keeps only lines with real content. ~~~python with open("draft.txt", "w") as f: f.write("alpha\n\nbeta\n \ngamma\n") with open("draft.txt") as f: words = [line.strip() for line in f if line.strip()] print(words, len(words)) with open("clean.txt", "w") as out: for word in words: out.write(word.upper() + "\n") with open("clean.txt") as f: print(f.read()) ~~~ - Lines 1 to 2: create a sample file with two blank lines, one of them made only of spaces. - Lines 3 to 4: for each line, keep line.strip() only when the stripped text is not empty. words becomes ['alpha', 'beta', 'gamma']. - Line 5: prints the list and its length, 3. - Lines 6 to 8: open clean.txt for writing and write each word in capitals, one per line. - Lines 9 to 10: read the result back: ALPHA, BETA, GAMMA. Here files live on a sandbox disk (see the Files tab). Each example and lesson starts from a fresh copy of the sample files, so experiment freely. ### Common mistakes - Forgetting "\n" in write(), so everything ends up on one line. - Opening with "w" when you meant "a": the old content is wiped. - Forgetting strip(), so every line keeps its "\n" and blank lines look non-empty. - Writing outside the with block: the file is already closed there. ### Recap - with open(name, mode) as f: opens a file and closes it for you. - f.read() gives the whole text; for line in f gives one line at a time. - Modes: "r" read, "w" overwrite, "a" append. f.write() adds no newline. - enumerate(items, start=1) numbers items as you loop.
py-modules: Python comes with a huge standard library: ready-made tools for maths, dates, counting, randomness, files and much more. Before writing a helper yourself, check whether it already exists there. It usually does. ### import: loading a module A module is a file of Python code you can reuse. import name loads it; then you reach what it contains with a dot: module.thing. ~~~python import math print(math.sqrt(16)) print(math.pi) print(math.floor(7.9), math.ceil(7.1)) ~~~ - Line 1: loads the math module. - Line 2: math.sqrt is the square root function: prints 4.0. - Line 3: math.pi is a value, not a function, so no brackets: 3.141592653589793. - Line 4: floor rounds down and ceil rounds up: 7 8. ### from ... import: taking just what you need from module import a, b brings in specific names, so you can use them without the module prefix. By the way, abs() needs no import at all: it is a built-in function that gives the distance from zero, so it drops the minus sign. ~~~python from math import sqrt, pi import random print(sqrt(25), round(pi, 2)) print(abs(-59), abs(59)) print(random.choice(["heads", "tails"])) print(random.randint(1, 6)) ~~~ - Line 1: imports only sqrt and pi, now usable by their bare names. - Line 2: loads random, for random picks. - Line 3: prints 5.0 3.14. - Line 4: abs gives 59 both times. - Line 5: random.choice picks one item of a list at random. Run it a few times. - Line 6: random.randint(1, 6) gives a whole number from 1 to 6, both included. ### Turning text into dates Dates often arrive as text, like "2026-03-01". The datetime module contains a type also called datetime. Its function strptime(text, format) ("string parse time") reads text according to a format. In the format, %Y means a 4-digit year, %m a 2-digit month and %d a 2-digit day; other characters, like -, must match exactly. ~~~python from datetime import datetime d = datetime.strptime("2026-03-01", "%Y-%m-%d") print(d) print(d.year, d.month, d.day) ~~~ - Line 1: imports the datetime type from the datetime module (same name, two different things). - Line 2: reads the text with the format. d becomes a datetime for 1 March 2026 at midnight. - Line 3: prints 2026-03-01 00:00:00. - Line 4: its parts are attributes, read with a dot: 2026 3 1. ### Date arithmetic: timedelta and .days Subtracting one datetime from another gives a timedelta: a duration. Its .days attribute is the number of whole days. If the first date is the earlier one, the result is negative, and abs() makes it positive. You can also add a timedelta to a date to move forward in time. ~~~python from datetime import datetime, timedelta fmt = "%Y-%m-%d" start = datetime.strptime("2026-02-20", fmt) end = datetime.strptime("2026-03-05", fmt) gap = end - start print(gap, gap.days) print((start - end).days, abs((start - end).days)) print(start + timedelta(days=30)) ~~~ - Line 2: stores the format once, to reuse it. - Lines 3 to 4: two datetimes. - Line 5: end - start is a timedelta. - Line 6: prints 13 days, 0:00:00 13. February 2026 has 28 days, and Python knows it, leap years included. - Line 7: the other way round gives -13; abs() turns it into 13. - Line 8: 30 days after 20 February is 2026-03-22 00:00:00. ### Counting with Counter Counter, from the collections module, counts how many times each item appears in a string (each character) or a list. It behaves like a dict of counts. most_common(n) returns the n most frequent items as a list of (item, count) tuples, biggest first. ~~~python from collections import Counter counts = Counter("banana") print(counts) print(counts["a"], counts["z"]) top = counts.most_common(1) print(top) print(top[0], top[0][0]) print("to be or not".replace(" ", "")) ~~~ - Line 2: counts each letter: b once, a three times, n twice. - Line 3: prints Counter({'a': 3, 'n': 2, 'b': 1}). - Line 4: read a count like a dict: 3. A missing item gives 0 instead of an error. - Line 5: most_common(1) returns a list holding one tuple. - Line 6: prints [('a', 3)]. - Line 7: top[0] is the tuple ('a', 3), and top[0][0] is the item itself: a. - Line 8: replace(old, new) returns a copy of a string with every old replaced by new. Replacing spaces with nothing removes them: tobeornot. ### Common mistakes - Using a module without importing it first: NameError. - Writing math.pi(): pi is a value, not a function. - A wrong format: %M means minutes, not months. Months are %m. - Forgetting .days: subtracting dates gives a timedelta, not a number. - Forgetting that most_common() returns a list of tuples, so you need two indexes to reach the item. ### Recap - import module then module.name, or from module import name. - datetime.strptime(text, "%Y-%m-%d") turns text into a date; subtracting dates gives a timedelta with .days. - abs() drops the minus sign. - Counter(...) counts items; most_common(1)[0][0] is the most frequent one.
py-classes: A class lets you create your own type of value, bundling data with the actions that work on it. A bank account has a balance (data) and accepts deposits (actions); a game character has a name and health points, and can move. ### A class and its objects class Name: defines a blueprint. Calling the class like a function, Name(...), builds an object (also called an instance) from it. A function defined inside a class is called a method. The special method __init__ (two underscores on each side, said "dunder init") runs automatically when an object is created. Its first parameter, self, is the new object; writing self.something = value stores an attribute: a variable that belongs to that object. ~~~python class Dog: def __init__(self, name, age): self.name = name self.age = age rex = Dog("Rex", 3) fido = Dog("Fido", 7) print(rex.name, rex.age) print(fido.name, fido.age) rex.age = 4 print(rex.age, fido.age) ~~~ - Line 1: starts the class Dog. Class names start with a capital letter by convention. - Line 2: the __init__ method, with self first, then the values we want. - Lines 3 to 4: store the arguments as attributes of the new object. - Line 5: Dog("Rex", 3) creates an object. Python calls __init__ with self set to that new object, name = "Rex" and age = 3. The finished object goes into rex. You never pass self yourself. - Line 6: a second, separate object. - Lines 7 to 8: read attributes with a dot: Rex 3 and Fido 7. - Line 9: attributes can be changed. - Line 10: prints 4 7: changing rex did not touch fido. ### Methods: behaviour that uses the object's data Other methods also take self first, so they can read and change the object's attributes. You call them with a dot, obj.method(arguments), and Python fills in self for you. ~~~python class Counter: def __init__(self): self.value = 0 def increment(self, step=1): self.value += step return self.value clicks = Counter() print(clicks.increment()) print(clicks.increment(5)) print(clicks.value) ~~~ - Lines 2 to 3: every new counter starts at 0. - Line 4: increment has a parameter step that defaults to 1. - Line 5: += adds to the attribute stored on this particular object. - Line 6: returns the new value to the caller. - Line 7: creates a counter. No arguments are needed, since __init__ only takes self. - Line 8: clicks.increment() runs the method with self = clicks: the value becomes 1, and 1 is printed. - Line 9: step is 5, so the value becomes 6: prints 6. - Line 10: reads the attribute directly: 6. ### Default values in __init__ __init__ is a normal function, so its parameters can have defaults too. And not every attribute has to come from a parameter: some can start with a fixed value. ~~~python class Player: def __init__(self, name, score=0): self.name = name self.score = score self.level = 1 ann = Player("Ann") bob = Player("Bob", 50) print(ann.name, ann.score, ann.level) print(bob.name, bob.score, bob.level) ~~~ - Line 2: score is optional and defaults to 0. - Line 5: level is not a parameter: every player starts at level 1. - Line 6: no score given, so ann.score is 0. - Line 7: bob.score is 50. - Lines 8 to 9: print Ann 0 1 and Bob 50 1. ### Protecting an object: check first, then change Methods are the right place to refuse bad requests. Check first, raise a ValueError if something is wrong, and only then change the attribute. Because raise stops the method immediately, a refused request leaves the object untouched. ~~~python class Thermostat: def __init__(self, target=20): self.target = target def set_target(self, degrees): if degrees < 5 or degrees > 30: raise ValueError("target must be between 5 and 30") self.target = degrees return self.target t = Thermostat() print(t.set_target(22)) try: t.set_target(80) except ValueError as e: print("Refused:", e) print(t.target) ~~~ - Lines 2 to 3: the target defaults to 20. - Lines 5 to 6: the check comes first. Out of range: raise, and the method stops. - Lines 7 to 8: only reached for valid values: update, then return the new target. - Line 9: creates a thermostat with target 20. - Line 10: 22 is valid: prints 22. - Lines 11 to 14: 80 is refused; the exception is caught and its message printed. - Line 15: prints 22: the failed call changed nothing. A method may need several checks one after the other, each with its own raise. Any failed check stops the method before the change happens. ### Common mistakes - Forgetting self as the first parameter of a method: Python complains about the number of arguments. - Writing balance = amount instead of self.balance = amount. Without self., it is a local variable that vanishes when the method ends. - Changing the attribute before checking, so a refused request still changes the object. - Misspelling __init__ (two underscores on each side), so it never runs. ### Recap - class Name: defines a type; Name(...) creates an object and runs __init__. - self is the object; self.attr = value stores data on it. - Methods are functions inside the class, called as obj.method(). - Validate, raise if needed, then change and return.
py-inherit: Inheritance lets one class reuse and adapt another. A circle and a rectangle are both shapes: they describe themselves the same way, but compute their area differently. You write the shared part once, in a parent class, and only the differences in each child. ### A subclass inherits everything Write class Child(Parent): to create a subclass. The child gets all the parent's methods for free. If the child defines a method with the same name, its own version is used instead: this is called overriding. ~~~python class Animal: def __init__(self, name): self.name = name def speak(self): return "..." def intro(self): return f"I am {self.name}" class Dog(Animal): def speak(self): return "Woof" class Fish(Animal): pass rex = Dog("Rex") nemo = Fish("Nemo") print(rex.intro(), rex.speak()) print(nemo.intro(), nemo.speak()) ~~~ - Lines 1 to 7: the parent class, with three methods. - Line 8: Dog(Animal) means a Dog is a kind of Animal. - Lines 9 to 10: Dog overrides speak. - Lines 11 to 12: pass means "nothing here": Fish adds nothing and keeps everything from Animal. - Line 13: Dog has no __init__ of its own, so Python uses Animal's: rex.name is "Rex". - Line 15: intro comes from Animal, speak from Dog: prints I am Rex Woof. - Line 16: Fish uses Animal's versions: prints I am Nemo .... ### Class attributes A variable written directly in the class body (not inside a method, not on self) is a class attribute: shared by every object of that class. Methods read it through self, just like a normal attribute. A subclass overrides it simply by giving it a new value in its own body. ~~~python class Vehicle: wheels = 4 def describe(self): return f"{self.wheels} wheels" class Bike(Vehicle): wheels = 2 print(Vehicle().describe()) print(Bike().describe()) print(Bike.wheels) ~~~ - Line 2: every Vehicle has 4 wheels. - Line 4: self.wheels looks on the object first, then on its class, then on the parent class. - Line 6: Bike overrides the value. - Line 7: Vehicle() creates an object (no __init__ is needed) and prints 4 wheels. - Line 8: the method comes from Vehicle, but self is a Bike, so self.wheels is 2: prints 2 wheels. - Line 9: you can read it from the class itself too: 2. ### Formatting numbers with :.2f Inside an f-string, a colon after the value adds a format. :.2f means "as a decimal number with exactly 2 digits after the point": it rounds if needed and adds zeros if missing. math.pi (from the math module) is the number pi, used for circles: the area of a circle is pi times the radius squared. ~~~python import math print(f"{math.pi:.2f}") print(f"{10:.2f}") print(f"{math.pi * 3 ** 2:.1f}") ~~~ - Line 2: prints 3.14. - Line 3: a whole number gets zeros: 10.00. - Line 4: the area of a circle of radius 3, with 1 decimal: 28.3. ### Parent methods that rely on the child Here is the real power. A parent method can call self.something(), and Python runs the version from the object's own class. So the parent writes the general recipe, and each child fills in its own detail. If a child forgets, the parent's version should complain: raise NotImplementedError is Python's standard way to say "a subclass must provide this". ~~~python class Employee: title = "Employee" def monthly_pay(self): raise NotImplementedError def summary(self): return f"{self.title} earns {self.monthly_pay():.2f}" class Salaried(Employee): title = "Salaried" def __init__(self, yearly): self.yearly = yearly def monthly_pay(self): return self.yearly / 12 class Hourly(Employee): title = "Hourly" def __init__(self, rate, hours): self.rate, self.hours = rate, hours def monthly_pay(self): return self.rate * self.hours print(Salaried(40000).summary()) print(Hourly(15.5, 120).summary()) try: Employee().summary() except NotImplementedError: print("Employee alone has no pay rule") ~~~ - Lines 1 to 6: the parent. monthly_pay only raises. summary uses self.title and the result of self.monthly_pay(), formatted with :.2f. - Lines 7 to 12: Salaried sets its own title, stores the yearly salary in its __init__, and overrides monthly_pay. - Lines 13 to 18: Hourly does the same with its own rule. Line 16 sets two attributes at once with tuple unpacking. - Line 19: summary runs Employee's code, but self is a Salaried object, so self.monthly_pay() is Salaried's: 40000 / 12. Prints Salaried earns 3333.33. - Line 20: 15.5 x 120 = 1860: prints Hourly earns 1860.00. - Lines 21 to 24: a plain Employee reaches the parent's monthly_pay, which raises NotImplementedError, caught here. ### super(): extending instead of replacing When a child overrides a method but still wants the parent's version to run, it calls super().method(...). This is used most often in __init__: the parent sets up its attributes, then the child adds its own. ~~~python class Animal: def __init__(self, name): self.name = name class Cat(Animal): def __init__(self, name, indoor): super().__init__(name) self.indoor = indoor tom = Cat("Tom", True) print(tom.name, tom.indoor) print(isinstance(tom, Cat), isinstance(tom, Animal)) print(issubclass(Cat, Animal)) ~~~ - Line 6: runs Animal's __init__, which sets self.name. - Line 7: then Cat adds its own attribute. - Line 9: prints Tom True. - Line 10: a Cat is also an Animal: True True. - Line 11: issubclass(child, parent) checks the classes themselves: True. ### Common mistakes - Writing class Circle: without (Shape): no inheritance at all. - Calling a method without self. inside another method: NameError. - Forgetting the brackets: self.area is the method itself, self.area() is its result. - Overriding __init__ in the child and forgetting super().__init__(...) when the parent sets up attributes. ### Recap - class Child(Parent): inherits every method and class attribute. - Defining a method or class attribute with the same name overrides it. - A parent method calling self.method() runs the child's version. - raise NotImplementedError marks a method children must provide; super() reaches the parent's version.
py-dunder: Why does + work on numbers and strings but not on your own objects? Python turns operators and some built-in functions into calls to methods with special names, surrounded by double underscores: dunder methods. Define them, and your objects work with +, ==, abs() and print() like built-in types. ### __repr__: how an object is shown By default, printing an object shows something unhelpful like <__main__.Plain object at 0x7f...>. A method __repr__(self) must return a string, and Python uses it whenever it needs to show the object: in print(), inside lists, and with the built-in repr(). ~~~python class Plain: def __init__(self, x): self.x = x class Point: def __init__(self, x, y): self.x = x self.y = y def __repr__(self): return f"Point({self.x}, {self.y})" print(Plain(1)) p = Point(1, 2) print(p) print([p, Point(0, 0)]) print(repr(p) == "Point(1, 2)") ~~~ - Lines 1 to 3: a class without __repr__. - Lines 8 to 9: Point's __repr__ returns text that looks like the code to build the object. - Line 10: Plain falls back to the default text, with a memory address. - Line 12: prints Point(1, 2). - Line 13: lists use it too: [Point(1, 2), Point(0, 0)]. - Line 14: repr(p) calls p.__repr__(). The text must match exactly, spaces included: True. ### __eq__: deciding when two objects are equal Without help, == on your objects is only True when both sides are the very same object. __eq__(self, other) lets you compare their contents: a == b becomes a.__eq__(b), so self is the left side and other the right side. ~~~python class Card: def __init__(self, rank, suit): self.rank = rank self.suit = suit def __eq__(self, other): return (self.rank, self.suit) == (other.rank, other.suit) a = Card(10, "hearts") b = Card(10, "hearts") c = Card(10, "spades") print(a == b, a == c) print(a != c) ~~~ - Line 6: packs both attributes into tuples. Two tuples are equal when all their items are equal, position by position. - Lines 7 to 9: three separate objects; a and b hold the same values. - Line 10: a == b runs a.__eq__(b): True. For a == c the suits differ: False. - Line 11: != automatically gives the opposite of __eq__: True. Without __eq__, a == b would be False, even though they look identical. ### __add__: making + work a + b becomes a.__add__(b). Return a new object built from both sides and leave the originals unchanged, just as 2 + 3 does not change the 2. ~~~python class Money: def __init__(self, cents): self.cents = cents def __add__(self, other): return Money(self.cents + other.cents) def __repr__(self): return f"Money({self.cents})" lunch = Money(1250) coffee = Money(300) total = lunch + coffee print(total) print(lunch, coffee) ~~~ - Lines 4 to 5: builds and returns a new Money holding the sum of both amounts. - Line 10: lunch + coffee calls lunch.__add__(coffee); total is a new object. - Line 11: prints Money(1550). - Line 12: the originals did not change: Money(1250) Money(300). ### __mul__: multiplying by a number a * b becomes a.__mul__(b). The right side does not have to be the same type: here it is a plain number. ~~~python class Money: def __init__(self, cents): self.cents = cents def __mul__(self, factor): return Money(self.cents * factor) def __repr__(self): return f"Money({self.cents})" ticket = Money(900) print(ticket * 3) print(ticket * 0.5) ~~~ - Line 4: factor is whatever stands to the right of *. - Line 9: prints Money(2700). - Line 10: prints Money(450.0): multiplying by a decimal gives a decimal. Writing the number first, 3 * ticket, would need yet another method; you only need object times number here. ### __abs__ and __len__: built-in functions Built-in functions call dunder methods too: abs(x) calls x.__abs__() and len(x) calls x.__len__(). For lengths on a flat grid, math.hypot(x, y) gives the straight-line distance from (0, 0) to (x, y): the square root of x squared plus y squared. ~~~python import math print(math.hypot(3, 4)) class Balance: def __init__(self, amount): self.amount = amount def __abs__(self): return abs(self.amount) class Playlist: def __init__(self, songs): self.songs = songs def __len__(self): return len(self.songs) print(abs(Balance(-40))) print(len(Playlist(["a", "b", "c"]))) ~~~ - Line 2: 3 squared plus 4 squared is 25, whose square root is 5: prints 5.0. - Lines 6 to 7: abs() on a Balance returns the absolute value of its amount. - Lines 11 to 12: len() on a Playlist returns its number of songs. - Line 13: prints 40. - Line 14: prints 3. Other useful ones: __lt__ for < (lets sorted() work), __contains__ for in, __str__ for a friendlier print(). ### Common mistakes - A __repr__ that does not match the expected text exactly, like Point(1,2) without the space. - Using print inside __repr__ instead of return. - Changing self inside __add__ or __mul__ instead of returning a new object. - Comparing only one attribute in __eq__. ### Recap - Dunder methods connect your class to Python's syntax: + calls __add__, * calls __mul__, == calls __eq__. - abs() calls __abs__, len() calls __len__, display uses __repr__. - Operators should return new objects. - math.hypot(x, y) is the length of (x, y).
py-gen: A generator produces values one at a time, only when asked. It is how Python reads huge files line by line or handles endless streams (sensor readings, new IDs, pages of results) without filling up memory. ### yield: a function that pauses Any function containing the keyword yield becomes a generator function. Calling it does not run its body: it returns a generator object. Each time you ask that object for a value with the built-in next(), the body runs until the next yield, hands out that value, and pauses right there, keeping all its variables. ~~~python def three_steps(): print("starting") yield "one" print("resuming") yield "two" yield "three" g = three_steps() print(g) print(next(g)) print(next(g)) print(next(g)) ~~~ - Line 7: nothing is printed: the body has not started. g is a generator object. - Line 8: shows something like <generator object three_steps at 0x...>. - Line 9: next(g) runs from the top: prints starting, reaches yield "one" and pauses. next returns "one", which is printed. - Line 10: resumes just after the first yield: prints resuming, then hands out "two". - Line 11: resumes again and hands out "three". One more next(g) would raise StopIteration: the generator has nothing left. ### Looping over a generator You rarely call next() yourself. A for loop asks for each value and stops cleanly at the end, and list() collects all the values into a list. ~~~python def countdown(n): while n > 0: yield n n -= 1 for x in countdown(3): print("tick", x) print(list(countdown(5))) gen = countdown(2) print(list(gen), list(gen)) ~~~ - Lines 2 to 4: while n is positive, hand out n, then (when resumed) decrease it. - Lines 5 to 6: print tick 3, tick 2, tick 1. - Line 7: prints [5, 4, 3, 2, 1]. - Line 8: one generator object. - Line 9: a generator can be used only once. The first list() empties it, so the second gives []. Call the function again for a fresh one. ### Infinite generators and islice Since values are computed only on demand, a generator may loop forever with while True:. The caller decides how many values to take. islice(generator, n), from the itertools module, takes just the first n. ~~~python from itertools import islice def odd_numbers(): n = 1 while True: yield n n += 2 print(list(islice(odd_numbers(), 5))) for value in odd_numbers(): if value > 7: break print(value) ~~~ - Line 4: while True: never ends on its own, but each yield pauses it. - Line 7: islice stops after 5 values: prints [1, 3, 5, 7, 9]. Never call list() on an endless generator without islice: it would never finish. - Lines 8 to 11: a for loop with break works too: prints 1, 3, 5, 7. ### Updating two variables at once Generators often keep their state in a few variables. a, b = x, y assigns several variables in one line. Python computes everything on the right first, using the old values, and only then assigns. That makes swaps and "new pair from the old pair" updates easy. ~~~python a, b = 1, 10 print(a, b) a, b = b, a print(a, b) a, b = b, a + b print(a, b) ~~~ - Line 1: a is 1, b is 10. - Line 3: the right side is (10, 1), so the values swap: a is 10, b is 1. - Line 5: the right side uses the old values: b is 1 and a + b is 11. So a becomes 1 and b becomes 11. - Line 6: prints 1 11. Writing a = b and b = a + b on two lines would give a different result, because the second line would already see the new a. ### yield inside a for loop yield can sit inside a for loop, handing out one result per round. Two helpers are useful here: range(start, stop, step) jumps by step, and a slice that goes past the end of a list simply stops at the end, with no error. ~~~python letters = ["a", "b", "c", "d", "e"] print(letters[3:10]) print(list(range(0, 10, 3))) def pairs(items): for i in range(len(items) - 1): yield (items[i], items[i + 1]) print(list(pairs(letters))) ~~~ - Line 2: only two items exist from index 3: prints ['d', 'e']. - Line 3: from 0, jumping by 3, below 10: [0, 3, 6, 9]. - Line 5: i goes from 0 to 3. - Line 6: hands out each item with its neighbour, as a tuple. - Line 7: prints [('a', 'b'), ('b', 'c'), ('c', 'd'), ('d', 'e')]. ### Generator expressions A comprehension written in round brackets instead of square ones is a generator expression: same syntax, but values come one by one instead of being stored in a list. Inside a function call, the extra brackets can be dropped. ~~~python squares = (n * n for n in range(5)) print(squares) print(sum(squares)) print(max(len(w) for w in ["fig", "banana", "kiwi"])) ~~~ - Line 1: nothing is computed yet. - Line 2: shows a generator object, not numbers. - Line 3: sum() pulls 0, 1, 4, 9, 16 one by one: 30. - Line 4: the longest word length: 6. ### Common mistakes - Using return instead of yield: the function hands back one value and ends. - Calling list() on an endless generator: it never finishes. - Reusing a generator that is already used up. - Updating two related variables on separate lines instead of a, b = .... ### Recap - yield turns a function into a generator that pauses between values. - next(), for and list() pull values out. - while True: plus yield makes an endless stream; islice takes a few. - a, b = b, a + b uses the old values on the right.
py-deco: A decorator adds extra behaviour to a function without touching the function's own code: logging every call, timing it, counting it, checking permissions. You switch it on with one line, @name, just above a def. ### Functions are values In Python a function is an object, like a number or a string. Its name without brackets refers to the function itself. You can store it in another variable, pass it to another function, and read its attributes, such as __name__, its name as text. ~~~python def shout(text): return text.upper() + "!" yell = shout print(yell("hello")) print(shout.__name__, yell.__name__) def apply_twice(func, value): return func(func(value)) print(apply_twice(shout, "hi")) ~~~ - Line 3: no brackets, so nothing runs: yell now refers to the same function as shout. - Line 4: calling yell runs shout: prints HELLO! - Line 5: both names lead to one function, which keeps its original name: shout shout. - Lines 6 to 7: func is a parameter holding a function. func(value) calls it, and the result is passed to it again. - Line 8: prints HI!! ### Functions inside functions A def can sit inside another function. The inner function can use the outer function's variables. The outer function can even return the inner function, which keeps remembering those variables. ~~~python def make_multiplier(n): def multiply(x): return x * n return multiply double = make_multiplier(2) triple = make_multiplier(3) print(double(5), triple(5)) print(double.__name__) ~~~ - Lines 2 to 3: the inner function uses n from the outer one. - Line 4: returns the inner function itself, not a result (no brackets). - Line 5: double is a multiply function that remembers n = 2. - Line 6: triple is another one that remembers 3. - Line 7: prints 10 15. - Line 8: its name is the inner function's: multiply. ### Passing arguments along with * and ** In a def, *args and **kwargs collect arguments. In a call, the stars do the reverse: *a_tuple spreads its items as positional arguments and **a_dict spreads its pairs as keyword arguments. Together, a function can accept anything and pass it on unchanged. ~~~python def describe(name, age, city="?"): return f"{name}, {age}, from {city}" values = ("Ada", 36) options = {"city": "London"} print(describe(*values, **options)) def pass_along(*args, **kwargs): print("args:", args, "kwargs:", kwargs) return describe(*args, **kwargs) print(pass_along("Bo", age=22)) ~~~ - Line 5: the same as describe("Ada", 36, city="London"). - Line 6: pass_along accepts any arguments at all. - Line 7: for the call on line 9, prints args: ('Bo',) kwargs: {'age': 22}. - Line 8: spreads them back out, exactly as received: describe("Bo", age=22). - Line 9: prints Bo, 22, from ? ### Writing a decorator A decorator is a function that takes a function and returns a new one, usually an inner wrapper that does something extra and calls the original. Writing @decorator on the line above a def is shorthand for name = decorator(name) right after it. ~~~python def announce(func): def wrapper(*args, **kwargs): print("Calling", func.__name__, "with", args) result = func(*args, **kwargs) print("Got", result) return result return wrapper @announce def add(a, b): return a + b total = add(2, 3) print(total) print(add.__name__) ~~~ - Line 1: announce receives the original function as func. - Line 2: wrapper accepts any arguments, so it fits any function. - Line 3: the extra behaviour, before the real call. - Line 4: calls the original with the same arguments and keeps its result. - Line 6: returns that result, so callers still get it. Without this line, the decorated function would return None. - Line 7: announce hands back the wrapper. - Lines 8 to 10: @announce means add = announce(add). From now on, the name add refers to the wrapper. - Line 11: runs wrapper(2, 3): prints Calling add with (2, 3), then Got 5. total is 5. - Line 13: prints wrapper: the original name is lost. ### functools.wraps: keeping the original name Tools and tests rely on __name__. The standard module functools fixes it: put @functools.wraps(func) above the wrapper's def. It copies the original's name (and description) onto the wrapper. It is itself a decorator, one that takes an argument. ~~~python import functools def announce(func): @functools.wraps(func) def wrapper(*args, **kwargs): print("Calling", func.__name__) return func(*args, **kwargs) return wrapper @announce def greet(name): return f"Hi {name}" print(greet("Ada")) print(greet.__name__) ~~~ - Line 3: decorates the wrapper with the identity of func. - Line 6: calls the original and returns its result in one line. - Line 11: prints Calling greet, then Hi Ada. - Line 12: prints greet: the name is kept. ### Attributes on functions Since functions are objects, you can attach your own attributes to them: func.something = value. A decorator can attach one to the wrapper once, then update it on every call, which is how information is kept between calls. Inside the wrapper, refer to it as wrapper.something. ~~~python import functools def remember_args(func): @functools.wraps(func) def wrapper(*args, **kwargs): wrapper.history.append(args) return func(*args, **kwargs) wrapper.history = [] return wrapper @remember_args def square(n): return n * n print(square.history) print(square(3), square(4)) print(square.history) ~~~ - Line 5: runs on every call: adds this call's arguments to the list. - Line 7: runs only once, when the decorator is applied: the wrapper gets an empty history list. It sits after the wrapper's def and outside its body, so it is not reset on each call. - Line 12: no calls yet: prints []. - Line 13: prints 9 16. - Line 14: prints [(3,), (4,)]. ### Common mistakes - Forgetting return wrapper: the decorated name becomes None. - Forgetting to return the original function's result from the wrapper. - Setting up a counter or list inside the wrapper body, so it starts over on every call. - Forgetting @functools.wraps(func), so __name__ says wrapper. ### Recap - Functions are values: pass them around, return them, give them attributes. - A decorator takes a function and returns a wrapper that calls it with *args, **kwargs. - @deco above def f means f = deco(f). - @functools.wraps(func) keeps the original name.
py-regex: A regular expression (regex) is a tiny pattern language for finding text by its shape: "some digits", "a word, an @, a domain", "two digits, a dash, two digits". It is how you pull emails, phone numbers, dates or IDs out of messy text. ### re.findall and raw strings Python's regex tools live in the module re. re.findall(pattern, text) returns a list of every piece of text that matches. In a pattern, \d means any digit from 0 to 9, and + after something means "one or more of it, as many as possible". Write patterns as raw strings, r"...": the r tells Python to leave backslashes alone, so \d reaches the regex engine untouched. ~~~python import re text = "Order 66 shipped 3 boxes on day 120" print(re.findall(r"\d", text)) print(re.findall(r"\d+", text)) print(re.findall(r"\d+", "no numbers here")) ~~~ - Line 3: \d alone matches single digits: ['6', '6', '3', '1', '2', '0']. - Line 4: \d+ grabs whole runs of digits: ['66', '3', '120']. Results are always strings. - Line 5: nothing matches, so the list is empty: []. ### More building blocks - \w: a word character (letter, digit or underscore). \s: whitespace (space, tab, newline). - \D, \W, \S: the capital letter means the opposite, for example \D is anything that is not a digit. - .: any single character. To match a real dot, escape it: \. - *: zero or more. {3}: exactly 3 times. Like +, they apply to the thing just before them. ~~~python import re s = "Ada_99 met Bo at 10.30, then Cy at 9.05" print(re.findall(r"\w+", s)) print(re.findall(r"\d+\.\d{2}", s)) print(re.findall(r"\d\d", "2026")) print(re.findall(r"a.", "banana bar")) ~~~ - Line 3: runs of word characters. The dot and the comma are not word characters, so 10.30 splits into '10' and '30'. - Line 4: digits, a real dot, then exactly two digits: ['10.30', '9.05']. - Line 5: two digits at a time: ['20', '26']. - Line 6: an a followed by any character, even a space: ['an', 'an', 'a ', 'ar']. ### Character sets with [ ] Square brackets match one character from a set: [aeiou] is a vowel, [0-9] a digit range, [\w.] a word character or a dot (inside brackets a dot is literal). A hyphen between two characters means a range, so to include a real hyphen, put it first: [-\w.]. Add + after the set for one or more. ~~~python import re mails = "Mail ana@shop.fr or ana.b@shop.fr" print(re.findall(r"[aeiou]", "regular")) print(re.findall(r"\w+@\w+\.\w+", mails)) print(re.findall(r"[\w.]+@\w+\.\w+", mails)) print(re.findall(r"[-\w]+", "a well-known e-mail")) ~~~ - Line 3: each vowel separately: ['e', 'u', 'a']. - Line 4: \w+ cannot cross the dot in ana.b, so the second match is cut: ['ana@shop.fr', 'b@shop.fr']. - Line 5: [\w.]+ accepts dots in the name part: ['ana@shop.fr', 'ana.b@shop.fr']. - Line 6: hyphen first in the set, so hyphenated words stay whole: ['a', 'well-known', 'e-mail']. Real addresses can also contain hyphens (as in help-desk.com) or plus signs: add them to the sets where they may appear. ### Groups: ( ) and (?: ) Round brackets group pieces, so a quantifier applies to the whole group: (ab)+ means "ab, repeated". But careful: with a normal group, findall returns only what the group matched, not the whole match. Write (?: ... ), a non-capturing group, to group without changing what findall returns. ~~~python import re log = "Start 08:58:12, error 09:02:45, end 10.05.11" print(re.findall(r"\d{2}(:\d{2}){2}", log)) print(re.findall(r"\d{2}(?::\d{2}){2}", log)) print(re.findall(r"\d{2}(?:[.:]\d{2}){2}", log)) ~~~ - Line 3: two digits, then the group "colon and two digits" twice. With a normal group, findall returns only the group's last match: [':12', ':45']. Not what we want. - Line 4: (?: makes a plain group, so whole matches come back: ['08:58:12', '09:02:45']. - Line 5: the separator is now a set, [.:], a dot or a colon, so the third time matches too. ### re.search and .group re.search(pattern, text) finds only the first match. It returns a match object, or None if nothing matches. On a match, .group(0) is the whole match and .group(1), .group(2) are the captured groups. ~~~python import re m = re.search(r"(\w+)@([\w.]+)", "contact: bo@acme.com today") print(m.group(0)) print(m.group(1), m.group(2)) print(re.search(r"\d", "no digits")) ~~~ - Line 2: two capturing groups: the name and the domain. - Line 3: prints bo@acme.com. - Line 4: prints bo acme.com. - Line 5: no match: prints None. ### re.sub: replacing matches re.sub(pattern, replacement, text) returns a copy of the text with every match replaced. Replacing with "" deletes the matches. Inside a list comprehension, it cleans a whole list. ~~~python import re print(re.sub(r"\s+", " ", "too many spaces")) print(re.sub(r"\D", "", "+33 (0)6-12")) codes = ["AB-12-CD", "EF 34 GH"] print([re.sub(r"[- ]", "", c) for c in codes]) ~~~ - Line 2: each run of whitespace becomes one space: too many spaces. - Line 3: every non-digit is deleted: 330612. - Line 5: hyphens and spaces removed: ['AB12CD', 'EF34GH']. ### Common mistakes - Forgetting the r before the pattern string. - Using a normal group with findall and getting only pieces back: use (?: ). - A bare . where you meant a real dot: write \.. - A hyphen in the middle of a set, which makes a range: put it first. ### Recap - re.findall lists all matches, re.search finds the first, re.sub replaces. - \d \w \s and their opposites \D \W \S; . any character; + * {n} repeat. - [...] is one character from a set; (?: ) groups without capturing.
py-boss: This final challenge combines classes, dictionaries, exceptions, comprehensions and files in one small program: an inventory manager that can save itself to disk and load itself back. Here are the last few tools you need. ### Dictionaries inside a dictionary A dict value can itself be a dict. It is a natural way to store records by name: the outer key is the item name, the inner dict holds its details. Chain the square brackets to reach inside. not in is the opposite of in. And or checks its left side first and stops as soon as something is true, so a test on a missing key can be guarded safely. ~~~python stock = {"pen": {"qty": 10, "price": 1.5}} stock["pen"]["qty"] += 5 stock["ink"] = {"qty": 2, "price": 9.99} print(stock) print(stock["ink"]["price"]) print("pad" in stock, "pad" not in stock) for name in ["pen", "pad"]: print(name, name not in stock or stock[name]["qty"] < 5) ~~~ - Line 2: stock["pen"] is the inner dict, and ["qty"] reaches inside it: 10 + 5 = 15. - Line 3: adds a new record under the key "ink". - Line 4: prints the whole nested dict. - Line 5: prints 9.99. - Line 6: in checks the outer keys: False True. - Lines 7 to 8: for "pen", the left side is false, so Python checks the quantity: 15 is not below 5, False. For "pad", the left side is already true, so Python never runs stock["pad"], which would raise a KeyError: prints True. ### setdefault: get it, or create it first d.setdefault(key, default) returns d[key] if the key exists. If not, it first stores default under that key, then returns it. It returns the stored dict itself, not a copy, so changing what it returns changes the record inside d. ~~~python stock = {"pen": {"qty": 10, "price": 1.5}} item = stock.setdefault("pen", {"qty": 0, "price": 2.0}) print(item) item = stock.setdefault("pad", {"qty": 0, "price": 4.0}) item["qty"] += 3 print(stock) ~~~ - Line 2: "pen" exists, so the existing record is returned and the default is ignored. - Line 3: prints {'qty': 10, 'price': 1.5}. - Line 4: "pad" is missing, so the default record is stored, then returned. - Line 5: changes the stored record through item. - Line 6: pad now has a quantity of 3 inside stock. An if name not in stock: check followed by a normal assignment does the same job, if you prefer. ### Looping over values and items .values() gives the inner dicts; .items() gives (key, value) pairs. Generator expressions inside sum() and sorted() build totals and filtered, sorted lists in one line. ~~~python stock = {"pen": {"qty": 10, "price": 1.5}, "pad": {"qty": 3, "price": 4.0}, "ink": {"qty": 1, "price": 9.99}} for name, info in stock.items(): print(name, info["qty"] * info["price"]) units = sum(info["qty"] for info in stock.values()) print(units) rare = sorted(name for name, info in stock.items() if info["qty"] < 4) print(rare) print(round(10 / 3, 2)) ~~~ - Lines 2 to 3: each pair is unpacked into the name and its record; prints the value of each line of stock. - Line 4: adds up the quantities: 10 + 3 + 1. - Line 5: prints 14. - Line 6: keeps the names whose quantity is below 4, then sorts them alphabetically. - Line 7: prints ['ink', 'pad']. - Line 8: round(x, 2) keeps 2 decimals, handy for money: 3.33. ### Saving and loading with json JSON is a text format for data that almost every language can read. json.dump(data, file) writes dicts, lists, strings, numbers and True/False into an open file; indent=2 makes it readable. json.load(file) reads it back as Python dicts and lists. ~~~python import json data = {"pen": {"qty": 10, "price": 1.5}, "tags": ["office", "cheap"]} with open("data.json", "w") as f: json.dump(data, f, indent=2) with open("data.json") as f: print(f.read()) with open("data.json") as f: loaded = json.load(f) print(loaded["pen"]["qty"], loaded == data) ~~~ - Line 1: loads the json module. - Lines 3 to 4: open a file for writing and dump the dict into it. - Lines 5 to 6: show the raw text: it looks almost like Python. - Lines 7 to 8: open the file again and turn the text back into a dict. - Line 9: prints 10 True: the round trip kept everything. ### @classmethod: building an object from a file A normal method receives an object as self. A method marked with the decorator @classmethod receives the class itself, by convention named cls, and is called on the class: Settings.from_file(...). Inside it, cls() creates a new object of that class. This is the standard way to write alternative ways of building an object, like loading one from a file. ~~~python import json class Settings: def __init__(self): self.values = {} def get(self, key): return self.values.get(key) @classmethod def from_file(cls, path): s = cls() with open(path) as f: s.values = json.load(f) return s cfg = Settings.from_file("config.json") print(type(cfg).__name__) print(cfg.get("app"), cfg.get("debug")) print(cfg.values["schedule"]) ~~~ - Lines 3 to 4: a new Settings starts with an empty dict. - Lines 5 to 6: a normal method that reads one value. - Line 7: @classmethod changes what the first parameter receives. - Line 8: cls is the class Settings itself. - Line 9: cls() runs __init__ and gives a fresh, empty object. - Lines 10 to 11: fill it from the JSON file. - Line 12: return the finished object. Forgetting this returns None. - Line 13: called on the class, not on an object. - Line 14: type(cfg) is its class, and __name__ its name: Settings. - Lines 15 to 16: values read from config.json: daily-report True, then the schedule dict. ### Common mistakes - Changing a quantity before checking it is allowed: check, raise, then change. - Reading d[name] before checking that name exists: put the not in test first. - Forgetting return at the end of a classmethod that builds an object. - Opening the file with "w" to load it: that empties it. ### Recap - Nested dicts: items[name]["qty"]; setdefault creates a record if missing. - sum(...) and sorted(...) with generator expressions summarise a dict. - json.dump(data, f, indent=2) saves, json.load(f) loads. - @classmethod gets cls; cls() builds a new object.
